# Evidence for the Helicity Barrier from Measurements of the Turbulence Transition Range in the Solar Wind

J. R. McIntyre ,1 C. H. K. Chen ,1 J. Squire ,2 R. Meyrand ,2 and P. A. Simon 1

1Department of Physics and Astronomy, Queen Mary University of London, London, E1 4NS, United Kingdom 2Department of Physics, University of Otago, 730 Cumberland Street, Dunedin 9016, New Zealand

(Received 15 July 2024; revised 19 February 2025; accepted 23 April 2025; published 8 July 2025)

Many hot, diffuse astrophysical plasmas are collisionless, with collision times that exceed dynamical timescales of interest. Without a standard viscosity, the mechanisms by which mechanical energy dissipates into heat via a turbulent cascade are complex and nonuniversal, with important consequences for the partition of heat between different species and directions. Recent theory has argued that in some parameter regimes a barrier to the turbulent cascade of energy forms at small scales, profoundly altering the nature of the heating of the plasma by changing how fluctuations dissipate. The solar wind is an environment, when in this parameter regime, where such a barrier would be expected to form. Here, using data from NASA’s Parker Solar Probe, we find that the shape of the magnetic energy spectrum around ion scales varies with solar wind parameters in a manner consistent with the presence of the barrier. This allows us to identify critical values of parameters necessary for the barrier to form; we show that the barrier appears fully developed for ion plasma beta of below ≃0.5 and becomes increasingly prominent with increasing normalized cross helicity (the difference in energy in wave packets propagating parallel and antiparallel to the background magnetic field) for values greater than ≃0.4. As these conditions are frequently met in the solar wind, particularly close to the Sun, our results suggest that the barrier is likely playing a significant role in turbulent dissipation in the solar wind and so is an important mechanism in explaining its heating and acceleration.

DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevX.15.031008 Subject Areas: Astrophysics, Plasma Physics

I. INTRODUCTION

The dissipation of a turbulent cascade is thought to be important for the dynamics of the solar wind and other astrophysical systems [1,2]. In the case of the solar wind it is proposed that it is responsible for its heating and acceleration [3–6]. However, the means by which this heating takes place remains a major open question. Unlike hydrodynamic turbulence, where the dissipation occurs due to viscosity, a range of processes can be involved in plasmas. Mechanisms suggested to be relevant for the solar wind include ion-cyclotron heating [7–9], stochastic heating [10,11], Landau damping [12–14], and magnetic reconnection [15,16]. The first of these, heating through the ion-cyclotron resonance (along with stochastic heating), has the advantage of being able to account for the ion temperature being greater than the electron temperature in the solar wind [17] and for ions being heated preferentially

in the direction perpendicular to the background magnetic field B0 [8]. Further, circularly polarized waves, which include electromagnetic ion-cyclotron waves (ICWs) that propagate in a direction near parallel to B0, are regularly observed in the near Sun solar wind [18,19]. However, it was for a long time not apparent how the solar wind turbulent cascade could transfer energy to small enough parallel scales to B0 to satisfy the ion-cyclotron resonance condition [20], as the cascade preferentially transfers energy to small perpendicular scales [21,22]. Meyrand et al. [23] proposed a novel “helicity barrier” mechanism which may enable such scales to be reached [24]. In this paper we use in situ solar wind data to investigate the presence of such a mechanism, and the conditions under which it occurs. The ion gyroradius,

ρi ¼ miv⊥;i jqijB ; ð1Þ

the radius of circular motion of an ion in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude B, where v⊥;i is the ion velocity perpendicular to the magnetic field, mi is the ion mass, and qi is the ion charge, is a crucial scale in

plasma dynamics. Motions at scales larger than ρi are mostly well described by magnetodynamics (MHD), while at smaller scales a single fluid description fails. For incompressible fluctuations, turbulence in MHD can be thought of in terms of the nonlinear interaction of wave packets propagating parallel and antiparallel to the background magnetic field. These two populations are the Elsasser fields, δz ¼ δv  δb, where δv is the perturbation to the velocity field and δb is the perturbation to the magnetic field in velocity units [25]. δzþ packets propagate antiparallel to B0 and δz−packets propagate parallel to B0. The difference in the energy of the two Elsasser fields, known as the cross helicity, is a conserved quantity in incompressible MHD, causing significant differences between balanced turbulence, where the energy of the two fields is comparable, and imbalanced turbulence, where it is not. For example, observations of solar wind turbulence have found the inertial range magnetic energy spectrum to become shallower for increasing cross helicity [26–30], and some theoretical models of imbalanced turbulence argue the cascade of one of the Elsasser fields is nonlocal in scales perpendicular to B0, meaning energy can be transferred between scales with large differences in size, unlike in balanced turbulence [31,32]. The solar wind is often observed to have high levels of cross helicity, particularly close to the Sun [33,34], making understanding this regime important for explaining its dynamics. The helicity barrier is an example of a mechanism possible only in imbalanced turbulence. Meyrand et al. [23] argue for the barrier using finite Larmor radius magnetohydrodynamics (FLR MHD), a fluid description of a plasma that, unlike MHD, is valid both above and below ρi. Such a description is necessary as the helicity barrier forms at scales ∼ρi, and does not exist within the MHD or reduced magnetohydrodynamics (RMHD) models, which do not capture ρi scale physics. It is thus a different process to MHD effects such as dynamic alignment or the reduction in nonlinearity at high normalized cross helicity [32,35,36]. In the limit of scales large compared to ρi, FLR MHD becomes RMHD, MHD in the limit of low-amplitude fluctuations elongated along B0. Analogous to MHD, FLR MHD supports two counterpropagating modes; these reduce to the RMHD Elsasser variables (as in MHD these are given by δz ¼ δv  δb) at large scales. The sum of the energy of these modes and a quantity proportional to their difference in energy, known as the “generalized helicity,” are conserved quantities in FLR MHD. At scales larger than ρi, the generalized helicity reduces to the cross helicity and undergoes a forward cascade, whereas at scales smaller than ρi, it is proportional to the magnetic helicity and undergoes a reverse cascade [37]. Meyrand et al. propose that these oppositely directed cascades create a barrier to the generalized helicity at the ion gyroradius, allowing only the balanced component of the energy cascade, jδzþj ∼jδz−j, for which the generalized

helicity is zero, to reach smaller scales. This limits the cascade rate of the dominant Elsasser field to match that of the other Elsasser field at electron scales. Squire et al. [24] argue that the buildup of energy at ion scales, as a result of the barrier to the cascade, may allow smaller parallel scales to be reached through critical balance (where the timescale for the propagation of Alfv´en waves equals that of the nonlinear turbulent timescale) than would otherwise occur if energy were more readily dissipated. This can then enable ion-cyclotron heating. Evidence that this is the case for imbalanced turbulence has been found in hybrid-kinetic simulations [24,38,39]. The lack of a constant energy flux when the helicity barrier is active, a fundamental difference from the standard picture of turbulence, would be expected to alter the shape of the energy spectrum. This may help explain the steep transition range in the magnetic spectrum between inertial and kinetic scales that is regularly observed in the solar wind [40–43]. Meyrand et al. [23] were able to produce a transition range in simulations for the first time. However, there are other suggested mechanisms for its formation, including Landau damping of kinetic waves [14], ion-scale coherent structures [44], or otherwise increased spectral transfer rates [42]. If the helicity barrier does play a role in the formation of the transition range, then the properties of that part of the spectrum should vary between regions of the solar wind where the barrier is expected to form and where it is not. Solar wind parameters which can be used to differentiate such regions include the following. (i) The ion plasma beta,

βi ¼ n0ikBT0i B2 0=2μ0 ; ð2Þ

where n0i is the mean ion number density, T0i the background ion temperature, and B0 is the background field strength. The helicity barrier can operate only at low βi, as the barrier results from the conservation of the total energy of the generalized Elsasser variables and the generalized helicity in FLR MHD, a description which is derived assuming βi ≪1. At βi ∼1 ions can couple with the energy cascade, an effect which, if strong enough, will break these conservation laws and prevent the barrier from forming. (ii) The normalized cross helicity,

σc ¼ hδzþ2 −δz−2i hδzþ2 þ δz−2i ; ð3Þ

which is the cross helicity normalized to the sum of the energy in the two Elsasser fields. Since the helicity barrier effect is caused by the inability of the (generalized) helicity to cascade below ρi, if there is

no flux of σc to small scales the turbulent cascade can proceed to small scales freely. Meyrand et al. [23] predict a critical normalized generalized helicity flux above which a barrier forms. Assuming that σc is related to this flux, as the normalized generalized helicity reduces to the normalized cross helicity at large scales, we therefore only expect the barrier to form for σc greater than a critical value and for the transition range to become increasingly prominent with increasing σc. Consistent with this, the transition range has previously been observed to be steeper for regions of greater cross helicity in the solar wind [45–47]. Meyrand et al. [23] and Squire et al. [38] also make an empirical prediction, based on simulations, that the perpendicular wave number of the break point between the inertial and transition range k⊥;1 varies with σc as k⊥;1ρi ≃ð1 −σcÞ1=4. Further, if the helicity barrier both results in dissipation by ICWs and plays a role in the formation of the transition range, then the properties of the transition range would be expected to correlate with the presence of ICWs. Consistent with this, the transition range has been observed to be steeper for intervals with higher levels of circular polarization [47,48]. In this paper, the dependencies of the location and slope of transition ranges of magnetic spectra, obtained using data from NASA’s Parker Solar Probe (PSP) [49,50], on solar wind parameters (normalized cross helicity, plasma beta, and degree of circular polarization) are shown to be consistent with the presence of the helicity barrier. The values of normalized cross helicity and ion plasma beta necessary for the barrier to form are identified, and further are found to be common in solar wind. This suggests the helicity barrier to be an important consideration for understanding solar wind heating.

II. DATA AND METHODS

PSP data from orbits 1–10 were used. The FIELDS instrument suite of PSP includes a search-coil magnetometer (SCM) and fluxgate magnetometers (MAG) [51]. The magnetic field data used were a merged SCM and MAG data set (SCaM) [52], to allow for spectra to be constructed across a greater range of frequencies than would be possible with either dataset alone. From orbit 2 onward data are not available for one axis of SCM so all total magnetic power spectra were obtained by summing the power spectra of only two axes. Signatures of PSP’s reaction wheels were identified and removed from the time series using a method similar to Shankarappa et al. [53]. The ion velocity and temperature data were provided by the SPAN-I instrument of the SWEAP instrument suite [54]. The velocity data were obtained through the bi-Maxwellian fits of Woodham et al. [55], being used only where available in this dataset and where at least 3 bins in the azimuth angle (ϕ) of SPAN-I were fitted to, with moments being used

otherwise. Fits were preferentially used over moments as they are less susceptible to error introduced by the fact that the velocity distribution of the solar wind is not always well captured by the field of view of SPAN-I [54]. Density data were obtained from quasithermal noise (QTN) measurements of the radio frequency spectrometer low frequency receiver [56]. The data were split into nonoverlapping 6-min intervals. Intervals where more than 1% of magnetic field data or 10% of velocity data were missing were removed. To account for error introduced by the SPAN-I field of view effect, any interval where the SPAN-I measured density was less than 10% of the QTN measured density was also discarded. A procedure similar to that of Shankarappa et al. [53] was used to reduce the impact of ICW signatures on the spectra analyzed. A time series of the degree of circular polarization,

σp ¼ 2 Imð ˜B1 ˜B 2Þ ˜B2 1 þ ˜B2 2 ; ð4Þ

where ˜B1 and ˜B2 are components of the magnetic field perpendicular to the local mean field in frequency space, was constructed for a discrete set of frequencies using wavelet transforms. Unmerged MAG data were used for this to provide access to data for all three axes. σp has an absolute value of 1 for purely circularly polarized waves, because ICWs are circularly polarized its value can therefore be used to identify intervals where they may be present. The final spectra were obtained from Morlet wavelet transforms over 100 scales of the SCaM magnetic field time series but with times and frequencies where jσpj > 0.7 discarded [19]. An example of spectra before and after this procedure was applied is shown in Fig. 1. Note the clear bump around 2 Hz in the preprocedure black spectrum, which is not present in the postprocedure blue spectrum. If this bump were not removed it would result in the transition range being measured to be artificially steeper than its true value, thanks to the presence of ICWs. After the reduction in the ICW signature was performed, a least squares regression procedure was used to fit each spectrum to a three power law function,

This removed intervals where the fit fails, as we expect αK < αT, but the 0.1 tolerance prevents intervals being discarded if there is simply not a clear transition range and so αT ∼αK. After all the filters described in this section were applied, 12334 intervals remained from an initial 24660 intervals.

III. RESULTS

A. Dependence of transition range index on cross helicity and plasma beta

If the helicity barrier mechanism is active in the solar wind, and it is responsible for the formation of the transition range, it follows that a more prominent transition range should be observed in regions of high normalized cross helicity and low ion plasma beta, as these are conditions necessary for the barrier to exist, according to the theory underpinning the barrier [23]. The dependencies of the transition range index on these parameters were therefore considered. Figure 2(a) shows the median value of the transition range spectral index αT for intervals binned by normalized cross helicity and ion plasma beta. The figure shows a clear trend of increasing αT with increasing jσcj. There also appears to be a tendency for αT to increase for decreasing βi, at least until lower values of βi are reached.

These are both consistent with predictions of the helicity barrier. Figure 2(b) shows the equivalent for αK and Fig. 2(c) for αT −αK. The former shows no apparent trend of αK on jσcj, in contrast to Bowen et al. [47]. However, that work measured αK, using a moving window, at kdi ¼ 10, considerably deeper into kinetic range than measured here (the mean high frequency break point for intervals used was k2di ∼2.7). The latter shows a tendency for αT −αK to increase with jσcj, demonstrating that it is not just that the transition range becomes steeper with greater normalized cross helicity, but that there is a stronger break between it

B. Dependence of transition index on degree of circular polarization

A further parameter considered was the degree of lefthanded circular polarization of the intervals σLH p . If the helicity barrier results in both the generation of ICWs, which are LH circularly polarized, and a more prominent transition range, then we should expect αT to be positivity correlated with σLH p . For each interval σp [Eq. (4)] was calculated as a function of frequency using fast Fourier transforms of the magnetic field components perpendicular to the mean field of the interval. As above, MAG data were used for this. The values of σp with a sign corresponding to left-handed polarization were then extracted and the resulting spectrum smoothed by averaging over a sliding window. This produced a measure of the degree of left-handed circular polarization against frequency. σLH p was defined to be the maximum value of this function for frequencies greater than half the low frequency break point f1. While the Doppler shift can cause the polarization measured in the spacecraft frame to invert from that of the plasma frame for waves with k · Vsw < 0 [19], the following results are not changed significantly if the absolute polarization is used rather than the left-hand polarization. Figure 5(a) shows the median value of αT for intervals binned by σLH p and jσcj, while Fig. 5(b) shows this for intervals binned by σLH p and βi (note that σLH p is calculated

from the magnetic time series without ICW signatures being removed and so values of greater than 0.7 are possible). There is a clear positive correlation between σLH p and αT, consistent with predictions of the helicity barrier. This correlation holds for both approximately constant jσcj or βi. This trend can again be seen in Fig. 6(a), which shows the mean value of αT for intervals binned by σLH p , with associated standard errors. It was verified that the behavior holds when the sampling angle or radial distance was held approximately constant, as was done for the trends found with jσcj and βi. Figure 6(b) shows this test for θBV, with each colored line of mean αT against σLH p corresponding to intervals from a sampling angle bin. While intervals with low θBV tend to have higher αT, as we also show in Figs. 3(b) and 4(b), the trend with σLH p remains. Figures 6(c) and 6(d) show the equivalent test for radial distance, with each colored line corresponding to a r bin. From Figs. 6(c) and 6(d) it is clear that the positive αT trend with σLH p also remains when distance is held approximately constant. The trend therefore appears robust.

2. Low frequency break point

The behavior of k⊥;1ρi was also considered. The presence of ICW signatures can make it unclear as to where the low frequency break should be placed, with f1 often being determined to be at frequencies a little higher than the peak of the ICW bump (as this is where the spectrum is particularly steep) before the procedure to remove the signatures is applied, and at the low frequency edge of the bump after the signatures have been removed (as this can introduce a kink to the spectrum). As a result, only intervals with σLH p < 0.5 were used when considering the behavior of k⊥;1ρi. For such intervals the break locations identified agree sufficiently well before and after the signatures were removed to give confidence in the results obtained. Indeed, there are no significant differences in the results obtained for the two sets of f1. A potential trend of decreasing k⊥;1ρi for increasing jσcj was found, which would be consistent with the barrier’s prediction. However, this trend was found not to hold when the conversion factor from f1 to k1ρi was held approximately constant, and so we cannot report this possible trend with confidence. As the predicted k⊥;1ρi ≃ ð1 −σcÞ1=4 trend is rather weak, it is perhaps unsurprising that it could not be untangled from dependencies on other solar wind parameters. Given the constraint on the value of σLH p of the intervals used, a trend with the degree of circular polarization was not considered.

IV. DISCUSSION

The results of this paper suggest the helicity barrier mechanism plays a significant role in the heating of the solar wind. We have shown that properties of the turbulence transition range vary with solar wind conditions in a manner consistent with the presence of the helicity barrier and have determined critical values of parameters necessary for the barrier to form. As the values of these parameters are common in the inner heliosphere, the barrier should be frequently active in the solar wind, thus resulting in the nature of its heating being dependent on solar wind conditions in a way that can help explain its observed properties. In order for the barrier to form βi must be sufficiently low for FLR MHD to be valid. We have shown, for the first time, that the spectral index of the transition range αT increases with decreasing ion plasma beta βi until reaching a plateau at around βi ≃0.5. This indicates that a value of βi ≃0.5 is sufficient for the mechanism to be fully active, a value commonly observed in the solar wind, particularly for regions close to the Sun. In regions of the highest βi considered a transition range was still observed, which may appear to contradict the condition that βi be low for the barrier to form. However, it is possible that multiple processes are responsible for generating the transition range and so this observation

does not exclude the presence of the barrier. As the behavior of the transition range found here cannot be explained by any of these other possible processes, as discussed below, they must be present alongside the barrier, if at all. Further, the largest plasma beta bin value that appears in this work is βi ∼2.2, which is relatively modest. Given this it may be the case that the conservation laws of FLR MHD are more robust than may have been expected, allowing the barrier to still form at these values of βi. It was also shown that intervals with high normalized cross helicity have steeper transition ranges than intervals of low cross helicity. This result is consistent with previous work [45–47], which we build on by demonstrating that it is not just that the transition range is steeper for regions of high jσcj, but that there is a stronger break with the kinetic range for regions of high jσcj. This behavior, where the steepening is restricted to around ion scales, rather than the whole kinetic range, is consistent with the helicity barrier acting at these scales. Unlike previous work, we made use of a procedure to reduce ICW signatures in the magnetic spectra analyzed and so were able to verify that the turbulent spectrum itself is steepening with increasing cross helicity, rather than the trend being the result of bumps introduced on top of the spectrum by ICWs, the presence of which is correlated with jσcj. We identified jσcj ≃0.4 as a critical value for the barrier, with αT being shown to clearly be increasing with normalized cross helicity for values greater than this. Once again this is a condition regularly met for intervals close to the Sun. It was further found that αT correlates positively with the degree of left-handed circular polarization σLH p , consistent with the transition range and the generation of ICWs both being possible results of the helicity barrier. This is consistent with previous work [47,48], but again we were able to verify that the spectrum itself is steepening by reducing ICW signatures. The behavior of the high frequency transition range break point k⊥;2ρi was also considered and found to robustly decrease with increasing σLH p . Such behavior may have been expected for the low frequency break point, as its predicted trend with normalized cross helicity suggests it may move to larger scales when the barrier is active, but no such behavior is predicted for k⊥;2ρi. A potential explanation for this is to consider σLH p as a proxy for dissipation through ion-cyclotron resonance, such that higher values of σLH p indicate a greater rate of dissipation. The dominant Elsasser field in high σLH p intervals may therefore dissipate to reach the power of the other Elsasser field at larger scales than for low σLH p intervals of similar normalized cross helicity. The transition range would hence end at a lower frequency, consistent with the observed trend. It is worth considering to the extent these results are consistent with alternative explanations for the formation of

the transition range. The steepening observed could be caused by the onset of dissipation by a mechanism other than by the ion-cyclotron resonance discussed throughout this paper, namely Landau damping [14] or stochastic heating [10,11]. However, neither of these mechanisms can account for the transition range being found to be steeper for regions with greater σLH p , as found here. Further, ion Landau damping becomes stronger for βi ≳1 [64], in contrast to the result here that the transition range becomes increasingly steep with decreasing βi. The transition range could also be caused by an increase in the spectral transfer rate [42] (by reconnection [16] or by the presence of coherent structures [44], for example) but, again, there is not an obvious candidate that can explain the correlation of transition range slope with the presence of ICWs. A more careful assessment of the parameter scalings of all of these different options could be performed, but that is beyond the scope of this work. Overall, a high degree of consistency between the helicity barrier and the behavior of the magnetic spectrum in the solar wind was found, increasing confidence in the barrier’s presence there. The rather modest critical values found of the parameters considered, βi ≲0.5 and jσcj ≳0.4, suggests the barrier is frequently active in the solar wind, making it an important consideration in understanding its heating. By causing greater amplitudes of the turbulent cascade to be achieved at ion scales than would otherwise be the case, the barrier may enable ion-cyclotron heating to take place, resulting in preferential heating of ions over electrons. This provides an explanation for ions being observed to be hotter than electrons in the solar wind. As the helicity barrier requires imbalanced turbulence to be active, the degree to which these processes would be expected to take place would depend on the cross helicity, which is known to be correlated with the wind speed. The barrier therefore also provides an explanation for the observed variation in the ratio of ion to electron temperature between fast and slow wind streams. Thus the dependencies introduced by the helicity barrier, by diverging from the standard turbulence picture of an unimpeded cascade to dissipation scales, have significant physical consequences. These consequences have the potential to help answer key open questions about the dynamics of the solar wind; this work supports the helicity barrier mechanism playing such a role. Future work could build on these results by measuring the spectra of the generalized Elsasser variables themselves. In regions that satisfy the conditions necessary for the barrier to form, as identified in this paper, a steep transition region should be observed in the spectrum of the dominant Elsasser field and the two Elsasser spectra should be balanced at scales smaller than this. Verifying that this is the case would provide a direct test that it is the imbalanced component of the energy that is being dissipated, as must be case if the helicity barrier is operating.
